lead.headline: Odisha Families Shelter From Cyclone Akvan
lead.deck: The storm reached land on Friday morning, weaker than feared.
body: This week, about 3.72 lakh people in Odisha left home for a while because a big storm was coming. A lakh is 100,000. Officials moved them to nearly 10,000 shelters, safe places to stay until the danger passed.

The storm, Cyclone Akvan, crossed the coast near Gopalpur on Friday morning, with gusts up to 90 km an hour. It was weaker than first forecast. A cyclone is a giant spinning storm that feeds on warm, wet air from the sea; over land, that fuel is cut off.

Among those moved to safety were 4,470 women expecting babies. Since then, 1,450 have given birth, and the mothers and newborns are safe. Odisha’s top official said there were no reports of people hurt or of major damage so far. Still, dozens of trains were cancelled, and more heavy rain is expected.

world.headline: Three Big Leaders Meet, but Ukraine Has No Seat
world.deck: Trump, Xi and Putin talked together in China for the first time.
body: The United States, China and Russia are three of the world’s most powerful countries. On Thursday their leaders, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, met as a group of three for the first time, in Shenzhen, a city in southern China.

They talked for about an hour and a half. Afterwards they shared a joint statement, a message all three agreed on. It promised to pump more oil and gas. It also said there can be no winners in a nuclear war, so one must never start.
Yet the statement did not mention the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Nobody from Ukraine was in the room, and Ukraine’s foreign minister said no decisions can be made without Ukraine.
Putin said Russia will not hold talks with Ukraine for now, after a Ukrainian attack on a bridge to Crimea. Trump gave the meeting 12 out of 10.

us.headline: Who Decides on War? A Close Vote in the Senate
us.deck: Senators turned down a plan about the war with Iran.
body: In America, the Constitution, the country’s founding rules, splits the power over war between Congress and the president.

On Thursday the Senate, one part of Congress, voted on a plan telling the president to take US armed forces out of the fighting with Iran. It lost, by 48 votes to 51. The House of Representatives, the other part of Congress, had already approved the plan in September.

Three Republicans voted for it and one Democrat against. Even if it had passed, it would not have gone to the president to sign, so it would mostly have been a message. Democrat Tim Kaine said the 3 November election showed the war is unpopular; Republican Thom Tillis called the plan “just a statement from Congress.” By 13 November, the war had cost at least $48.3 billion.
us.why: In a vote this close, a few senators changing sides can decide the result.

india.headline: India and Japan Team Up on Supplies
india.deck: Ministers met in Tokyo to plan safer supplies.
body: India and Japan want to make sure no single country can cut off the supplies their economies depend on, such as computer chips and medicines.

On Thursday, two ministers from each country met in Tokyo, Japan’s capital, for 90 minutes. A meeting like this is called a “2+2.” They agreed to build stronger supply chains, the paths goods travel from makers to users, for computer chips, critical minerals, clean energy and medicines. Their joint statement warned about countries using trade to pressure others, without naming any country.

They also agreed to work together on defence: Japan’s forces will be allowed to train with missiles on Indian firing ranges. Each country also supports the other’s wish for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Japan has promised to invest about $62.5 billion in India over ten years, and the next 2+2 meeting will be held in India.
india.why: Shared supplies make it harder for one country to cut off things people need.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to The Breakfast Table for Friday, November 20. Today: how families in India stayed safe from a cyclone, three world leaders at one table, and a close vote in America.
Let’s start in India. What happened with Cyclone Akvan?

A cyclone is a giant spinning storm. Akvan crossed the coast near the town of Gopalpur, in Odisha, on Friday morning. Before it arrived, about 3.72 lakh people moved to nearly 10,000 shelters. A lakh is 100,000.
Was the storm as strong as people feared?
No. It was weaker than first forecast, with gusts up to 90 kilometres an hour. A cyclone feeds on warm, wet air from the sea. Over land, that fuel is cut off.
And what about the families in the shelters?

Among those moved to safety were 4,470 women expecting babies. Since then, 1,450 have given birth, and the mothers and newborns are safe. Odisha’s top official said there were no reports of people hurt or of major damage so far. Still, dozens of trains were cancelled, and more heavy rain is expected.
Next, a meeting in China. Who was there?

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. On Thursday they met as a group of three for the first time, in Shenzhen, a city in southern China. They talked for about an hour and a half.
Did they agree on anything?
They shared a joint statement, which is a message all three agreed on. It promised to pump more oil and gas. It also said there can be no winners in a nuclear war, so one must never start.
Did they talk about the war in Ukraine?

The statement did not mention it, and nobody from Ukraine was in the room. Ukraine’s foreign minister said no decisions can be made without Ukraine. Putin said Russia will not hold talks with Ukraine for now.
Finally, America. What did the Senate vote on?

In America, the Constitution splits the power over war between Congress and the president. On Thursday the Senate, one part of Congress, voted on a plan that would have told the president to take US armed forces out of the fighting with Iran.
Did it pass?

No. It lost, by 48 votes to 51. Three Republicans voted for it, and one Democrat voted against it. Even if it had passed, it would not have gone to the president to sign, so it would mostly have been a message.
So a few senators changing sides could have made the difference.
That’s right. In a vote this close, a few senators changing sides can decide the result.
